Further, the model makes predictions that can be experimentally tested. This is valuable for the field of gene regulation.

Essential revisions:

All three reviewers agreed the work addresses a major question in the field but also raised important issues that should be addressed. These primarily revolve around how the model is described, and the extent to which the full parameter space is explored. Further, the authors have not explored alternative models which would help clarify how surprising and robust their results are. There is also an opportunity to emphasize that the proposed model is not necessarily absolutely correct, but one of many plausible models that can produce a non-linear relationship between genome structure (enhancer-promoter contact) and transcription. Any thoughts on other models that could generate similar dynamics would be a useful discussion point.

1. The presentation of the model is unclear. It is currently present in the text, lines 110-122, in pure qualitative description. Authors define only rates in the text; definitions of other model parameters are not present. For example, E and a are not specifically defined in the text or Methods section. Since both terms "enzyme" and "enhancer" are being used and in fact "enzyme tagging" and "enhancer tagging" occur simultaneously in the model, it is not possible to say for sure when do authors call which one in the model and thus the methods section can be interpreted in different ways. Moreover, the cartoon is missing a legend confirming, which molecular player is which. The figure caption mentions only green triangles being the tags, but no other parts of the cartoon are being explained. Taken together, this makes it very difficult to verify the mechanics of the model.

– Given its centrality to the manuscript, we recommend describing the overall strategy in more detail in Results. For example, at line 124 (Pg. 4) the authors could talk about how the simulations are done, including where the variability comes from (e.g., random starting conditions vs. probabilistic events vs. different parameters).

– – The authors should provide a detailed technical description of their model directly in the text, including description of their parameters, list their constitutive equations and identify all parameters in their cartoon Figure 1C.

– Axes labels in all figures should be expressed in the parameters/variables of the model (as in Figure 6C-D) directly connecting to inputs/outputs of the model.

2. In the Methods section, it appears that in lines 577-580 of the model description, the mass is not conserved. This issue is critical to address, because when mass is not conserved the model can not be physical.

3. Xiao et al. make several key assumptions to dramatically simplify their model. Namely, it is assumed that promoter modification and transcription are equivalent and that enhancer-promoter contact influences transcription instead of transcription influencing structure. Steady-state equilibrium must also be assumed. It would be helpful if the authors explicitly stated these assumptions and provided references to support their being reasonable.

4. For clarity, it would be helpful to discuss model parameters in greater detail. First, we suggest noting which parameters shift the location of the curve and which increase the steepness of the curve. Second, we recommend including a phase diagram exploring when sigmoidal behavior and any other key model predictions arise across parameter space. In what circumstances does hypersensitivity or time lag emerge? The authors demonstrate that a narrow set of parameters is sufficient to produce a super-linear relationship between enhancer-promoter contact and transcription in Figure 6. One potential dilemma is this model's ability to explain many experimental observations by indicating that minimal changes all occur in the sub-linear regime while observable changes occur in the super-linear regime. Given that one needs specific parameters to replicate an example of the hyper-linear regime (including at least three degrees of stimulation and increasing stimulation of the successive states), it could be valuable to demonstrate how large the plausible parameter space is. Without an exhaustive search across the space of minimal parameters, it is not clear when this property emerges or how common it is within the full parameter space. The authors could vary model parameters and plot a grid visualizing behavior (e.g., steepness of the curve or Hill coefficient).

5. The authors observe hysteresis in median transcription rate as a function of enhancer contact frequency. However, the presented violin plots suggest a presence of two states, one with low and one with high transcription rates. In the intermediate regime of enhancer contact frequency, where authors report hysteresis, the violin plots show bimodal distributions suggesting coexistence of these two states. This would suggest that the system exists in and switches between two distinct states with a discontinuous transition, instead of a continuous hysteretic behavior as suggested by the median behavior.

6. There is also an opportunity to emphasize that the proposed model is not necessarily absolutely correct, but one of many plausible models that can produce a non-linear relationship between genome structure (enhancer-promoter contact) and transcription. Any thoughts on other models that could generate similar dynamics would be a useful discussion point. There are parallels to both sigmoidal dose-response curves, where drug concentration is plotted against response, and transcription factor binding curves, where free ligand concentration is plotted against the fraction bound. We recommend providing background context on these types of models or the Hill equation to illustrate why non-linear behavior is or is not surprising given the proposed model.

7. It is not totally clear why the authors decide to call their proposed approach the futile cycle model. There are similarities to other well-known models in biochemistry and biophysics that should be noted. It might make sense to simply call this a mechanistic model of cooperative promoter activation. If the authors stick with "futile cycle", the relationship between promoter activation through tags and metabolic signaling should be described in more detail.

8. At the beginning of the Discussion section authors state they will propose future experiments in each section. However, in some of the sections it is not clear what specifically authors are proposing. These suggestions should be made clearer.

9. If I understand the model correctly, the non-linearity arises because of the increase rate of tag addition when tag is already present. The authors then speculate histone modifications can be one such tag. However, there is only so many sites of modification at a promoter. Can the authors analyze how the possible range of tag densities affects performance of the model? Is the range required biologically plausible?

10. Can the authors do more analysis to explore how rapid changes in gene expression may occur (e.g. upon signaling a gene may go up within minutes)? How much more frequent does the E-P interaction need to be for rapid switch to the active promoter state? Can the authors do an analysis where they change the rates of the futile cycle upon some signal: at what time scale does transcription then change (keeping E-P frequency the same)?

11. Due to the lack of description, in many sections it is not clear what are the specific inputs and outputs of the model (e.g. Figure 2).

12. The Methods section describes the chemical kinetics of the suggested reactions and the insulation score calculations. But it is not clear how do these inform each other, how are contact-frequency maps chosen/computed and cross-referenced with the local E-P kinetics?

13. In 587-588, the index of k is 2(n+1), which equals to 2n+2, but then in the next line the following assumption is made 2n+1 → n+1.

14. The authors make assumptions that their kinetic considerations hold for n>2. What is the evidence?

15. The language of the paper is often not technically precise with qualifiers missing, which could lead to ambiguities and misinterpretations. Here are some examples:

p. 1, line 10, "difference in contact across TAD borders is usually less than twofold";

p. 1, line 17, "results from recent cohesion disruption";

p. 2, line 71, "A simple model of hypersensitivity to changes in contact frequency".

16. On p. 13, line 483, authors define Ostwald ripening as given by weak multivalent interactions; however, Ostwald ripening is a thermodynamic process. In addition, they propose that liquid condensates become larger due to Ostwald ripening, but there are also other processes that may occur, such as coalescence of condensates, which would also lead to larger condensates.

17. An alternative explanation for TAD-specific enhancer action is that an E-P interaction within a TAD (between two convergent CTCF sites), one that is brought about by extruding cohesin, is not equivalent to an interaction that occurs between two loci on either side of a CTCF site and that can be a random collision that is not mediated by extruding cohesin. In other words, two interactions can be of the same frequency but can be of a very different molecular nature. I agree that this model would not explain the results of the experiment where cohesin is acutely removed.

18. In the beginning of the introduction the authors introduce TADS. I recommend that the authors present this in a more nuanced way: compartment domains also appear as boxes along the diagonal, an issue that has led some in the chromosome folding field to be confused. This reviewer believes TADS are those domains that strictly depend on cohesin mediated loop extrusion, whereas compartment domains are not. If the authors agree, perhaps they can rewrite this section?

claims.source: This simple model version includes a regime in which condensate size (a proxy for transcription) is hypersensitive to changes in 3D structure, as illustrated by simulations of the Markov jump process (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through stochastic simulations shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Hypersensitive behavior in the GTF condensate model requires cluster size greater than 2.
claims.source: We saw that sensitivity increased with cluster size, and hypersensitive behavior required cluster size greater than 2 (Figure 3E).

results.result: TADs are genomic domains with higher intra-domain than inter-domain 3D proximity, detectable by multiple techniques, and represent a statistical property emerging from dynamic conformational states rather than static structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C8, C9, and C10 establish well-supported background knowledge about TADs based on extensive prior literature. These are established findings in the field with multiple independent experimental validations cited.

results.result: TAD border deletion at the Ubx/abd-A locus causes only 1-2.5-fold increase in E-P contact frequency but results in 5-fold increase in gene expression, demonstrating hypersensitive transcriptional response to small structural changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C17-C21 present quantitative analysis of published ORCA data (Mateo et al., 2019) showing the disconnect between modest contact frequency changes and large transcriptional effects. The analysis includes both population-level and single-cell data, ruling out technical artifacts. The quantification is clearly presented in Figure 1 with appropriate statistical support.

results.result: TAD boundaries correlate with gene expression patterns and their disruption by cis-mutation causes disease-associated expression changes, yet global TAD disruption by cohesin depletion causes minimal transcriptional changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C14 accurately summarize prior experimental findings from multiple cited studies. This establishes the paradox motivating the authors' modeling work. The claims are well-supported by the cited literature, though the authors are reporting others' findings rather than generating new data.

results.result: Enhancers act on promoters in cis requiring physical proximity, yet recent single-cell and live-cell measurements show little correlation between E-P proximity and transcription activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C15, C16, C53-C55 accurately describe another key paradox from recent literature. The claims are well-supported by multiple cited experimental studies using different methodologies (fixed-cell and live-cell imaging). This establishes a second major motivation for the modeling work.

results.result: Existing models fail to explain the hypersensitive response of gene expression to small changes in contact frequency.
results.evaluation: Claim C5 is supported by the authors' analysis of existing literature and the quantitative disconnect demonstrated in claims C3-C4 and C17-C21. This motivates the need for new theoretical frameworks.

results.result: A two-state enhancer model exhibits only sublinear responses to TF concentration, while a three-state model with two binding sites can be hypersensitive when koff2/kon2 < koff1/kon1.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C23 present mathematical analysis of simple enhancer models shown in Figure 2. The derivations follow standard chemical master equation approaches and the conditions for hypersensitivity are correctly identified. The mathematical reasoning is sound.

results.result: The enhancer cooperativity model is rejected because observed contact frequency changes upon TAD boundary perturbation are insufficient to explain transcriptional changes.
results.evaluation: Claim C24 is supported by comparison of the cooperativity model predictions with the experimental data presented in Figure 1. The authors correctly identify that the magnitude of cooperative contact changes is too small to account for the observed transcriptional effects.

results.result: Futile cycle models based on either GTF condensates or PTM accumulation at promoters can achieve hypersensitive transcriptional responses to small changes in E-P contact frequency, with hypersensitivity requiring cluster/tag size greater than 2.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C25-C28 present the core theoretical contribution. The models are mathematically well-defined (Figures 3B-C, 3H-I), simulations demonstrate hypersensitivity (Figures 3D, 3J), and parameter sweeps identify conditions for hypersensitivity (Figure 3E-G). The models are grounded in known biochemical mechanisms with experimental support cited (C27). The mathematical framework is rigorous and the simulations are reproducible with provided code.

results.result: Promoters with different intrinsic properties (condensate dissolution or tag removal rates) can respond differently to the same E-P contact change, creating apparent E-P specificity through different tipping points rather than biochemical lock-and-key mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30 and C43-C44 demonstrate an important prediction of the futile cycle models through simulations (Figure 4). The models show how promoter-intrinsic parameters can create differential responses to identical structural perturbations, offering a mechanistic explanation for observed E-P specificity without requiring specific biochemical recognition. The logic is sound and simulations support the conclusions.

results.result: Futile cycle models exhibit hysteresis, with qualitatively different transcriptional sensitivities at short versus long time scales, showing weak changes at early time points despite sufficient perturbation to eventually drive state transitions.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33 demonstrate hysteresis in both model versions through simulations (Figures 5C-G). The time-dependent behavior is clearly shown with appropriate parameter choices. The mathematical basis for hysteresis in futile cycle systems is well-established, and the simulations correctly demonstrate this property.

results.result: The futile cycle models show weak correlation between E-P contact and transcription at the single-cell level (odds ratios 1.0-1.3), matching experimental observations, with correlation becoming detectable only with large sample sizes (~20,000 cells), demonstrating that contact-dependent regulation need not produce strong single-cell correlation.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C38 and C56-C58 address the third paradox through simulations (Figure 6). The models correctly predict weak odds ratios matching experimental data (C34, Figure 6D), show no detectable temporal correlation with moderate sample sizes (C36, Figure 6F-G), and reveal weak but significant correlations with large samples (C37, Figure 6H-I). The mechanistic explanation (C57) follows logically from the model structure. This provides a compelling resolution to the apparent contradiction between contact-dependent regulation and lack of single-cell correlation.

results.result: The futile cycle model provides unified explanations for four key observations: weak TAD boundaries having major regulatory effects, gene insensitivity to some structural changes, differential effects of global versus local disruption, and lack of single-cell E-P distance-transcription correlation.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42 synthesize the implications of the modeling results for resolving the paradoxes established earlier. Each explanation follows logically from the demonstrated properties of the futile cycle models (hypersensitivity, differential tipping points, hysteresis, and weak single-cell correlation). The claims represent valid interpretations of the modeling results.

results.result: Recent experimental studies show nonlinear/hypersensitive transcriptional responses to E-P distance variation, consistent with futile cycle model predictions.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 cite recent experimental studies that support the model predictions. The cited work (Yokoshi et al., 2020; Despang et al., 2019; Zuin et al., 2021) provides independent experimental validation of hypersensitive responses to E-P contact frequency changes. The authors accurately represent these findings.

results.result: The timing difference between cohesin degron experiments (hours) and genetic deletion experiments (days/generations) may explain their different transcriptional outcomes, with longer intervals showing greater changes consistent with hysteresis predictions.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 propose an explanation for the differential effects of global versus local TAD disruption based on hysteresis and timing. While the model demonstrates hysteresis (C31-C33) and the timing difference is factually correct, the explanation remains somewhat speculative. The authors acknowledge this is their interpretation and note complications from different cellular backgrounds. Additional experimental validation would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: GTF condensates (Med1, PolII, Brd4) show stability exceeding imaging time in reported studies.
results.evaluation: Claim C52 accurately reports findings from cited experimental studies on condensate stability. This provides some support for the timescales assumed in the condensate model version, though the authors appropriately note that condensate existence and detection remain controversial.

results.result: Futile cycles of repressive condensates or tags could also account for hypersensitivity at some promoters.
results.evaluation: Claim C59 is a logical extension of the model framework. The mathematical structure would support repressive mechanisms with transcription inversely proportional to tag/condensate levels. This is appropriately presented as a plausible alternative rather than a demonstrated result.

results.result: Through accumulation of tags or GTFs in condensates, promoters integrate their history of regulatory element interactions and respond nonlinearly to structural changes.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 synthesizes the key conceptual insight from the modeling work. This interpretation follows directly from the demonstrated properties of the futile cycle models and represents the central mechanistic proposal of the paper.
